paper_metadata.title: Microstructure and defect effects on strength and hydrogen embrittlement of high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi processed by high-pressure torsion

evidence.quote: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are considered as new hydrogen compatible materials, but enhancing their yield strength without deteriorating their hydrogen embrittlement resistance is challenging. In this study, various kinds of defects are introduced into a CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy by plastic straining via the high-pressure torsion method

An equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting under an argon atmosphere using pieces of elements with purity levels higher than 99.5%. After induction melting, disc-shaped samples (10 mm diameter and 1 mm thickness) were cut from the ingot using the wire-cut electrical discharge machining (EDM) technique, homogenized at 1273 K for 1 h and quenched in iced water.
After straining through 1/16 HPT turns, grains are still at the micrometer level, while many deformation twins appear.
After small straining via 1/8 HPT turns, the hydrogen content increases to 10.1 wt.ppm.
A further increase in strain through 1/4 HPT turns leads to the formation of dislocation cells as well as some ultrafine grains.
With further increase in the strain by HPT processing for 1 turn, the microstructure completely transforms to a nanograined structure
such a nanograined structure remains reasonably unchanged with increasing the number of HPT turns to 10

The HPT process was carried out on the polished samples with a thickness of 0.8 mm at room temperature (T = 300 K), under an applied pressure of P = 6 GPa for N = 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 5 and 10 turns with 1 rpm rotation speed.

The initial coarse-grained sample absorbs a small amount of 3.0 wt.ppm of hydrogen.
After small straining via 1/8 HPT turns, the hydrogen content increases to 10.1 wt.ppm.
With the formation of nanograins after HPT processing for 10 turns, the hydrogen content reaches 26.8 wt.ppm
Twins is a major deformation mechanism at the early stages of straining, resulting in over 1 GPa yield strength and 9% elongation in the presence of hydrogen.
those contained twins and low-mobility dislocations show a good combination of high yield strength over 1 GPa and hydrogen embrittlement resistance with up to 9% elongation
Due to a low stacking fault energy of the Cantor alloy, deformation twinning is the main deformation mechanism when the grain sizes are large
Such an increase should be due to the contribution of grain boundary diffusion which is faster than lattice diffusion and can result in a higher hydrogen content for a given period
Catastrophic failure of hydrogen-charged nanograined samples indicates that a transition in the hydrogen embrittlement mechanism from HELP to HEDE should have occurred

These results suggest that twins and defects with low mobility such as Lomer-Cottrell locks and D-Frank partial dislocations are effective to achieve a combination of high yield strength and good hydrogen embrittlement resistance by suppressing the hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity in HEAs.
The increase in the yield stress with HPT processing is naturally due to the formation of lattice defects and grain refinement
The Lomer-Cottrell locks, which are formed by encountering two dislocations on a slip plane, are sessile on the slip plane and can act as barrier for other dislocations
